newsitem.title: USA: Judge allows key videotape in Kevorkian trial.
newsitem.headline: Judge allows key videotape in Kevorkian trial.

text.p: Jack Kevorkian's latest bid to thwart assisted suicide charges was quashed on Friday when a judge ruled that a key videotape allegedly showing a woman asking him to help her die can be admitted as evidence against him.

Ionia County Circuit Judge Charles Miel also on Friday dismissed assisted suicide charges against Kevorkian's associate, Janet Good, who is dying of pancreatic cancer. Neither Kevorkian nor Good were at the hearing.
Both decisions on Friday were seen as blows to Kevorkian's defence in his fourth assisted sucide trial, which is scheduled to start on June 10 in this small western Michigan town.
Kevorkian is charged with violating unwritten Michigan common law by assisting the Aug. 30, 1996, suicide of Loretta Peabody, a 54-year-old Ionia woman suffering from multiple sclerosis.

Authorities had believed that Peabody died of natural causes until the videotape turned up in an August 6, 1996, police raid of a suburban Detroit motel room, where Kevorkian was meeting with another patient who took her life the next day.
The tape is the prosecutors' key piece of evidence linking Kevorkian to Peabody.

Kevorkian's lawyer, Geoffrey Fieger, argued that it was obtained illegally. He said Bloomfield Township police had no reason to suspect that any illegal activity was about to occur at the Quality Inn where Kevorkian was meeting with Isabelle Correa and family members.
"We wanted to end this case today. The reason we didn't want the tapes (as evidence) is that we wanted to end it," Fieger said adding that the trial will waste taxpayers money.

Miel sided with the Bloomfield Township police officers who testified that their past experience with Kevorkian's use of the same motel led them to believe that an assisted suicide was about to happen.
A motel clerk testified that he became suspicious and called police after Correa checked in with three other people because she was confined to a wheelchair and all of them "looked depressed."

Good, 73, a long-time Kevorkian supporter and associate who hosted an assisted suicide last year at her Farmington Hills, Mich., home, was originally scheduled to stand trial with Kevorkian. She was diagnosed with terminal cancer last year, and some legal experts have said she would generate sympathy for Kevorkian if put on trial next to him.
But Ionia County Prosecutor Raymond Voet argued that given her illness, she might not be able to withstand the trial or to even attend it. Miel dismissed the charges against Good.

Kevorkian, who has publicly admitted to attending 45 suicides since 1990, has been tried and acquitted on assisted sucicide charges three times in cases involving five deaths, once in 1994 and twice in 1996.
